title: The effectiveness of protective behavioral strategies for reducing alcohol use and alcohol-related harms among adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

claims.statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023 (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, did not detectably change how much people said they drank (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, a step not described as planned); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, all outcomes were self-reported and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those effects cannot be credited to the strategies. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).
